subject: science
statement: Using body parts like handspans is a perfectly accurate way to measure length.
why: Students rely on their own bodies as the most immediate and accessible measuring tools in daily life.
fix: Body parts vary in size from person to person, so they cannot provide a consistent or standard measurement for everyone.

probe.question: If you and your friend measure the same table using handspans, will you get the same number?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because a handspan is a fixed unit of length.

subject: science
statement: You must always start measuring from the very edge of the ruler.
why: Students often confuse the physical edge of the scale with the zero mark.
fix: Measurement should start from the zero mark, as the edge of the scale might be broken or worn out.

probe.question: If the zero mark on your scale is broken, how do you measure an object?
probe.wrong_answer: I cannot measure it because the scale is broken at the start.

subject: science
statement: An object moving in a circle is not changing its position.
why: Students often equate 'motion' only with moving from one place to another in a straight line.
fix: Motion is any change in position over time, regardless of whether the path is straight or curved.

probe.question: Is a stone tied to a string and whirled around in a circle in motion?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it stays in the same area and doesn't go anywhere.

subject: science
statement: Periodic motion must always involve a back-and-forth movement.
why: Students often overgeneralize the example of a pendulum to all periodic motions.
fix: Periodic motion is any motion that repeats itself at regular intervals, such as the rotation of the Earth or a fan blade.

probe.question: Is the motion of the blades of a ceiling fan periodic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it does not move back and forth like a pendulum.

subject: science
statement: The moon is a luminous object because it shines at night.
why: Students confuse the act of being visible with the act of producing light.
fix: The moon is non-luminous; it only reflects the light coming from the sun.

probe.question: Which of these produces its own light: a candle, a mirror, or the moon?
probe.wrong_answer: The moon and the candle.

subject: science
statement: Transparent objects are invisible.
why: Students associate 'transparent' with 'not there' because they can see through it clearly.
fix: Transparent objects are physical materials that allow light to pass through them, but they are still visible due to reflections and edges.

probe.question: If a glass window is transparent, can you see the window itself?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because light goes right through it.

subject: science
statement: Light can bend around corners to reach dark areas.
why: Students observe light filling a room and assume it curves to reach all parts.
fix: Light travels in a straight line and cannot turn corners unless it is reflected by a surface.

probe.question: If you shine a torch into a bent pipe, will the light come out the other end?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, light will bend to follow the shape of the pipe.

subject: science
statement: A shadow is a dark image of the object itself.
why: Students view the shadow as a 'copy' or 'ghost' of the object rather than an absence of light.
fix: A shadow is simply an area where light is blocked by an opaque object; it does not contain details of the object.

probe.question: Does a shadow of a person show their eyes and nose?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if the shadow is clear enough.

subject: science
statement: A battery is a source of electricity that gets used up and disappears.
why: Students observe that batteries stop working after some time and assume the physical substance inside is consumed or lost.
fix: A cell converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy; it does not disappear but runs out of chemical potential.

probe.question: Where does the electricity go when a battery dies?
probe.wrong_answer: It is all used up and has vanished into the air.

subject: science
statement: Electricity flows from the battery to the bulb, but not back to the battery.
why: Students often view the battery as a 'source' that pushes energy out, similar to how a tap pushes water out.
fix: Electricity requires a continuous, unbroken path (a closed loop) from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, and back to the other terminal.

probe.question: Why do we need two wires connected to the bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: One wire is enough to carry the electricity to the bulb to make it glow.

subject: science
statement: The switch consumes electricity to turn the light on.
why: Students confuse the function of a switch as a 'power' device rather than a simple mechanism to break or complete a path.
fix: A switch does not consume electricity; it simply acts as a bridge that connects or disconnects the path for current to flow.

probe.question: What happens to the electricity when you turn the switch off?
probe.wrong_answer: The switch absorbs the electricity so it doesn't reach the bulb.

subject: science
statement: Only metals can conduct electricity.
why: Textbooks often use metal wires as the primary example, leading students to overgeneralize.
fix: While most metals are good conductors, other materials like graphite or salty water can also conduct electricity.

probe.question: Can a pencil lead (graphite) conduct electricity in a circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not a metal.

subject: science
statement: All shiny metal objects are magnetic.
why: Students often associate the metallic luster of objects like coins or aluminum foil with the properties of iron.
fix: Only specific materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt are attracted to magnets; many other metals are not.

probe.question: Will a magnet attract a shiny aluminum spoon?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is made of metal.

subject: science
statement: Magnets attract all objects.
why: Students often see magnets picking up various things in toys and assume the attraction is universal.
fix: Magnets only attract materials that have magnetic properties; they do not affect plastic, wood, or glass.

probe.question: Will a magnet pick up a plastic pen?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, magnets attract everything.

subject: science
statement: The middle of a magnet is the strongest part.
why: Students confuse the physical center of the object with the location of the magnetic force.
fix: The magnetic force is concentrated at the two ends, called poles, and is weakest in the middle.

probe.question: Where will the most iron filings stick to a bar magnet?
probe.wrong_answer: In the middle of the magnet.

subject: science
statement: Opposite poles repel each other.
why: Students often confuse the terminology of 'opposite' with 'repulsion' due to linguistic similarity.
fix: Like poles repel each other, while opposite poles attract each other.

probe.question: What happens when you bring a North pole near a South pole?
probe.wrong_answer: They push each other away.

subject: science
statement: The compass needle points North because it is attracted to the North Pole of the Earth.
why: Students assume the 'North' pole of the magnet is attracted to the 'North' pole of the Earth.
fix: The North pole of the compass needle is attracted to the Earth's magnetic South pole, which is located near the geographic North.

probe.question: Why does the compass needle point North?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the North pole of the magnet likes the North pole of the Earth.

subject: science
statement: Heat and temperature are the same thing.
why: In everyday language, people use the words interchangeably when describing weather or cooking.
fix: Temperature measures how hot or cold an object is, while heat is the total energy transferred between objects due to a temperature difference.

probe.question: If you add more hot water to a cup, does the heat increase or the temperature?
probe.wrong_answer: The heat increases because the water is hot.

subject: science
statement: Objects have heat inside them.
why: Students often perceive heat as a substance or fluid that resides within an object rather than energy in transit.
fix: Heat is energy that is moving from a warmer object to a cooler one; objects contain internal energy, not 'heat'.

probe.question: Where does the heat go when you take a hot spoon out of tea?
probe.wrong_answer: The heat stays inside the spoon for a while.

subject: science
statement: Cold moves from the ice to the hand.
why: Language like 'the cold is coming in' suggests cold is an active agent that travels, similar to heat.
fix: Cold is simply the absence of heat; heat always moves from the warmer object to the cooler one.

probe.question: Why does your hand feel cold when holding an ice cube?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the cold from the ice moves into my hand.

subject: science
statement: Metals are naturally warm to the touch.
why: Students touch a metal object and feel it is colder than wood, leading them to think metal has a 'cold' property.
fix: Metal is a good conductor, so it draws heat away from your hand faster than wood, making it feel colder.

probe.question: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a plastic spoon in the same room?
probe.wrong_answer: Because metal is a cold material and plastic is a warm material.

subject: science
statement: Heat only rises upwards.
why: Students observe smoke or hot air rising and overgeneralize this to all heat transfer.
fix: Heat can travel in any direction; convection currents occur in fluids because hot fluid becomes less dense and rises, but radiation travels in all directions.

probe.question: If you hold your hand to the side of a candle flame, why do you feel heat?
probe.wrong_answer: I shouldn't feel heat because heat only goes up.

subject: science
statement: Dark clothes absorb heat from the sun, but light clothes do not.
why: Students confuse 'absorbing heat' with 'creating heat', thinking light clothes have a property that repels heat.
fix: All objects absorb some radiation, but dark colors are better absorbers and emitters of heat than light colors.

probe.question: Do light-colored clothes absorb any heat from the sun?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they reflect all the heat and don't absorb any.

subject: science
statement: Time is an absolute concept that exists independently of any periodic event.
why: Students experience time as a continuous flow in daily life without needing to observe a clock.
fix: Time is measured by counting the repetitions of a periodic event, such as the swing of a pendulum or the rotation of the Earth.

probe.question: If all clocks and watches in the world stopped, would time still exist?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, time would keep passing exactly the same way.

subject: science
statement: A pendulum takes longer to complete a swing if it is pulled further away.
why: Students confuse the distance traveled (amplitude) with the time period of the oscillation.
fix: For small oscillations, the time period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length, not on the amplitude.

probe.question: If you pull a pendulum bob further to the side before releasing it, what happens to the time it takes to complete one oscillation?
probe.wrong_answer: It will take more time because it has to cover a longer distance.

subject: science
statement: An object that moves faster always covers more distance in the same amount of time.
why: Students often fail to distinguish between the concept of speed as a rate and distance as a total quantity.
fix: Speed is defined as the distance covered per unit time; if an object is faster, it covers more distance in a specific time interval.

probe.question: If two cars travel for the same amount of time, how do we know which one is faster?
probe.wrong_answer: The one that traveled the longest distance is the fastest.

subject: science
statement: Uniform motion means the object is moving in a straight line.
why: The word 'uniform' is often associated with straightness or lack of change in direction in everyday language.
fix: Uniform motion means an object moves along a straight line with a constant speed, meaning it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

probe.question: If a car moves in a circle at a constant speed of 40 km/h, is it in uniform motion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because its speed is constant.

subject: science
statement: The shape of a distance-time graph is a picture of the path the object took.
why: Students tend to interpret graphs as literal maps or sketches of the physical trajectory of the object.
fix: A distance-time graph represents the relationship between distance and time, not the physical path or shape of the road.

probe.question: If a car travels on a curved road, what will its distance-time graph look like?
probe.wrong_answer: The graph will be curved like the road.

subject: science
statement: A battery provides current to the circuit, and the wire just acts as a path for the current to travel.
why: Students often view the battery as the sole source of electricity and ignore the closed-loop requirement.
fix: Current only flows when there is a complete, unbroken path from one terminal of the battery to the other.

probe.question: If you connect a bulb to only one terminal of a battery, will it light up?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the battery provides the electricity.

subject: science
statement: Electricity is used up as it flows through a bulb.
why: The word 'consumption' in everyday language leads students to think current is a fuel that gets exhausted.
fix: Current is a flow of charge; the same amount of current that enters a bulb leaves it, but energy is transformed into light and heat.

probe.question: Is the current flowing out of a bulb less than the current flowing into it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the bulb uses up some of the current.

subject: science
statement: Only high-power appliances like heaters get hot, while wires and bulbs do not.
why: Students only notice heat when it is the intended function of the device.
fix: All conductors offer some resistance to current, which causes them to heat up, though it may be too small to notice in thin wires.

probe.question: Does a connecting wire get warm when a bulb is lit?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the heater coil gets warm.

subject: science
statement: A fuse is a device that stores extra electricity to prevent a power surge.
why: Students confuse the fuse with a battery or a capacitor due to the term 'safety device'.
fix: A fuse is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows, preventing damage.

probe.question: What happens to the fuse when there is a short circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: It releases extra electricity to keep the circuit running.

subject: science
statement: An electromagnet is a permanent magnet that is powered by electricity.
why: Students assume that because it is called a 'magnet', it must always have magnetic properties.
fix: An electromagnet is only magnetic when current is flowing through the coil wrapped around the core.

probe.question: What happens to an electromagnet when you switch off the current?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays a magnet but becomes weaker.

subject: science
concept: Rectilinear propagation of light and reflection
statement: Light travels only from the source to the object, not to the eye.
why: Students often focus on the light source as the active agent and ignore the role of the eye in receiving reflected light.
fix: We see objects because light reflects off them and enters our eyes.

probe.question: Why can you see a book in a dark room if you turn on a torch?
probe.wrong_answer: The torch light hits the book and stays there so the book becomes visible.

subject: science
concept: Rectilinear propagation of light and reflection
statement: A mirror adds something to the object to create an image.
why: Students perceive the image as a physical entity existing behind the mirror rather than a reflection of light.
fix: The image is just light rays reflecting off the mirror surface to our eyes, creating the appearance of an object behind it.

probe.question: Where does the image go when you move away from the mirror?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays behind the mirror waiting for me to come back.

subject: science
statement: Concave mirrors always make objects look smaller.
why: Students often generalize their experience with the back of a spoon (convex) to all curved surfaces.
fix: Concave mirrors can make objects look larger or smaller depending on how close the object is to the mirror.

probe.question: What happens to your face if you look into a concave makeup mirror from very close?
probe.wrong_answer: It looks smaller than my actual face.

subject: science
statement: A lens works by blocking some light to create an image.
why: Students confuse the bending of light (refraction) with the blocking of light (shadows).
fix: Lenses change the direction of light rays by bending them as they pass through the glass.

probe.question: How does a magnifying glass make things look bigger?
probe.wrong_answer: It blocks the extra light around the edges so only the middle part is seen.

subject: science
concept: Real vs Virtual images and Dispersion
statement: A real image is one that is physically present on the screen.
why: Students interpret 'real' as a solid object rather than a collection of light rays focused at a point.
fix: A real image is formed where light rays actually meet on a screen, but it is still just light, not a physical object.

probe.question: If you touch the screen where a real image is projected, what will you feel?
probe.wrong_answer: I will feel the object that is being projected.

subject: science
concept: Real vs Virtual images and Dispersion
statement: A prism adds colors to white light.
why: Students see the colors coming out of the prism and assume the prism is the source of the color.
fix: White light is actually a mixture of many colors, and the prism just separates them.

probe.question: Where do the rainbow colors come from when white light passes through a prism?
probe.wrong_answer: The glass of the prism contains those colors and paints the light.

subject: science
statement: An object in motion must have a force constantly acting on it.
why: Students confuse the state of motion with the cause of motion based on everyday experiences like pushing a cart.
fix: A force is only needed to change the state of motion of an object, not to maintain a constant speed.

probe.question: If you stop pushing a moving toy car, why does it stop?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the force pushing it is gone, so it cannot move anymore.

subject: science
statement: Forces only exist when there is visible movement.
why: Students equate force with visible physical work or displacement.
fix: Forces can act on objects without causing motion, such as when you push a heavy wall that does not move.

probe.question: Is there a force acting on a book resting on a table?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the book is not moving.

subject: science
statement: Gravity is a force that only acts on objects falling downwards.
why: Students associate gravity only with the act of falling rather than a constant pull towards the Earth's center.
fix: Gravity is a non-contact force that acts on all objects at all times, pulling them towards the center of the Earth.

probe.question: Does gravity act on a ball while it is moving upwards?
probe.wrong_answer: No, gravity only pulls it down once it starts falling.

subject: science
statement: Pressure is the same as force.
why: In everyday language, the terms are often used interchangeably to describe how hard something is pushed.
fix: Pressure is defined as the force acting on a specific unit of surface area; it depends on both the force and the area.

probe.question: Why is it easier to cut vegetables with a sharp knife than a blunt one?
probe.wrong_answer: Because you apply more force with the sharp knife.

subject: science
statement: Atmospheric pressure only pushes downwards.
why: Students visualize air as a heavy blanket resting on top of things.
fix: Atmospheric pressure acts in all directions because air molecules move randomly and collide with surfaces from all sides.

probe.question: Does the air exert pressure on the underside of a table?
probe.wrong_answer: No, air pressure only pushes down on the top surface.

subject: science
statement: Friction is caused only by the roughness of surfaces.
why: Students often focus on visible bumps and ignore the molecular-level interactions between smooth surfaces.
fix: Friction is caused by the interlocking of irregularities on surfaces, which exists even on surfaces that appear smooth to the naked eye.

probe.question: Why does a highly polished glass slide still have friction?
probe.wrong_answer: It doesn't have friction because it is perfectly smooth.

subject: science
statement: Friction is a force that only acts on moving objects.
why: Students associate friction with the act of sliding or moving, failing to recognize static friction.
fix: Friction acts on stationary objects as well, preventing them from starting to move when a small force is applied.

probe.question: Is there any friction acting on a heavy box sitting on the floor if I push it slightly but it doesn't move?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the box is not moving.

subject: science
statement: The area of contact between two surfaces affects the amount of friction.
why: Everyday intuition suggests that a larger object 'grabs' more surface area, leading to more friction.
fix: Friction depends on the nature of the surfaces and the normal force (weight), not the surface area of contact.

probe.question: If you place a brick on its side versus its flat face, which one experiences more friction?
probe.wrong_answer: The flat face, because it has more area touching the ground.

subject: science
concept: Types of Friction: Static, Sliding, and Rolling
statement: Rolling friction is a type of friction that is stronger than sliding friction.
why: Students confuse the ease of movement with the magnitude of the force, or assume that 'more parts touching' means more friction.
fix: Rolling friction is significantly weaker than sliding friction, which is why wheels are used to move heavy loads.

probe.question: Why is it easier to pull a suitcase with wheels than to drag it on the floor?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the wheels have more friction to grip the ground.

subject: science
statement: Friction only happens between solid surfaces.
why: Students define friction based on solid-solid contact and do not perceive air or water as 'surfaces'.
fix: Fluids like air and water also exert a frictional force on objects moving through them, known as drag.

probe.question: Does an airplane experience friction while flying through the air?
probe.wrong_answer: No, friction only happens when things touch the ground.

subject: science
concept: Sound as a result of vibration
statement: Objects must be moving visibly to produce sound.
why: Students associate sound with large, obvious movements like a drum skin or a swinging bell.
fix: Sound is produced by rapid back-and-forth movements called vibrations, which are often too small or fast to see with the naked eye.

probe.question: Does a stationary tuning fork produce sound?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not moving at all.

subject: science
statement: Sound can travel through a vacuum or empty space.
why: Students often confuse sound with light, which does not require a medium to travel.
fix: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires particles of a material medium like air, water, or solids to transfer energy.

probe.question: If an explosion happens in outer space, would you hear it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because sound travels everywhere.

subject: science
statement: Loudness and pitch are the same thing.
why: In everyday language, people often use 'high' or 'low' to describe both volume and musical notes.
fix: Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration, while pitch depends on the frequency of vibration.

probe.question: If you hit a drum harder, does the pitch change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it gets higher because it is louder.

subject: science
statement: A high-pitched sound always travels faster than a low-pitched sound.
why: Students overgeneralize the idea that 'stronger' or 'higher' things have more speed.
fix: The speed of sound depends on the medium, not on the frequency or amplitude of the sound wave.

probe.question: Which travels faster, a high-pitched whistle or a low-pitched drum beat?
probe.wrong_answer: The whistle, because it has a higher pitch.

subject: science
statement: The ear canal is a hollow tube that carries sound directly to the brain.
why: Students often view the ear as a simple pipe rather than a complex system of energy conversion.
fix: The ear converts sound vibrations into mechanical vibrations in the eardrum, which are then converted into electrical signals by the inner ear for the brain.

probe.question: What happens to sound waves once they enter the ear canal?
probe.wrong_answer: They travel straight through the tube to the brain.

subject: science
statement: All liquids conduct electricity equally well.
why: Students often think of liquids as a single category like solids or gases without considering chemical composition.
fix: Only liquids containing dissolved salts, acids, or bases (electrolytes) conduct electricity; pure water is a poor conductor.

probe.question: Will distilled water light up an LED in a tester?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because all water conducts electricity.

subject: science
statement: Electricity flows through liquids just like it flows through metal wires.
why: Students visualize current as a flow of electrons in all materials, ignoring the role of ions in liquids.
fix: In liquids, electricity is carried by the movement of charged particles called ions, not by free electrons as in metals.

probe.question: How does current move through a salt solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Electrons jump from one end of the wire to the other through the liquid.

subject: science
statement: The chemical change in a liquid happens only at the battery, not at the electrodes.
why: Students associate the power source as the sole cause of all changes in a circuit.
fix: Chemical reactions occur specifically at the surfaces of the electrodes where the current enters and leaves the liquid.

probe.question: Where do bubbles form during the electrolysis of water?
probe.wrong_answer: Near the battery terminals.

subject: science
statement: Electroplating is just painting a metal with a liquid metal.
why: Students confuse the physical appearance of a shiny coating with the process of painting.
fix: Electroplating is a chemical process where metal ions from a solution are deposited onto an object using electric current.

probe.question: How does copper get onto a spoon during electroplating?
probe.wrong_answer: The spoon is dipped in liquid copper paint and dried.

subject: science
statement: The metal being coated disappears into the solution and is gone forever.
why: Students struggle with the conservation of matter in chemical reactions.
fix: The metal ions in the solution are replenished by the anode, maintaining a balance in the electrolyte.

probe.question: What happens to the copper plate (anode) during copper plating?
probe.wrong_answer: It just sits there and does not change.

subject: science
concept: Static Electricity and Charging by Rubbing
statement: Only insulators can be charged by rubbing.
why: Students often see experiments with plastic scales and balloons, leading them to think conductors cannot hold a charge.
fix: Conductors can also be charged by rubbing, but the charge flows away quickly if they are held by hand; they must be insulated to retain the charge.

probe.question: If you rub a metal rod with a silk cloth, does it acquire a charge?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because metal is a conductor and only insulators can be charged.

subject: science
concept: Static Electricity and Charging by Rubbing
statement: Rubbing creates new electric charges.
why: The word 'charging' implies the creation of something new rather than the transfer of existing particles.
fix: Rubbing does not create charge; it only transfers existing electrons from one object to another, leaving one positive and one negative.

probe.question: Where do the charges on a balloon come from after you rub it on your hair?
probe.wrong_answer: The rubbing process creates new charges on the surface of the balloon.

subject: science
statement: Lightning is caused by the friction between clouds and the air.
why: Students often oversimplify the 'rubbing' concept learned in static electricity to explain all electrical phenomena.
fix: Lightning is caused by the accumulation of massive amounts of charge due to the movement of air currents and water droplets within the cloud, leading to a discharge between clouds or to the ground.

probe.question: How does a lightning bolt form in the sky?
probe.wrong_answer: The clouds rub against the air and create static electricity like a balloon on hair.

subject: science
statement: Lightning always strikes the tallest object in an area.
why: Common safety advice emphasizes avoiding tall trees, leading students to believe the tallest object is a magnet for lightning.
fix: Lightning follows the path of least resistance to the ground; while tall objects are more likely to be hit, it is not a rule that it must be the tallest.

probe.question: If there is a small pole and a tall tree in an open field, will lightning definitely hit the tree?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, lightning always strikes the tallest object in the vicinity.

subject: science
statement: Earthquakes are caused by the earth opening up and swallowing things.
why: Movies and cartoons often depict the ground splitting into deep chasms during an earthquake.
fix: Earthquakes are vibrations or shaking of the earth's crust caused by the sudden movement or collision of tectonic plates deep underground.

probe.question: What happens to the ground during a major earthquake?
probe.wrong_answer: The ground splits open and creates a big hole that swallows buildings.

subject: science
statement: Tectonic plates are floating on a liquid ocean of magma.
why: Textbooks often use the analogy of 'floating' to describe plates, which students interpret as being on a liquid surface like a boat.
fix: Tectonic plates move over the semi-molten, plastic-like layer of the mantle, not a liquid ocean; the movement is extremely slow and driven by heat currents.

probe.question: How do tectonic plates move?
probe.wrong_answer: They float on top of a liquid layer of magma like ships on the ocean.

subject: science
statement: Objects become visible because our eyes send out rays to touch them.
why: Students often confuse the act of looking with an active process of 'reaching out' to objects.
fix: We see objects because light from a source reflects off the object and enters our eyes.

probe.question: Why can't you see a book in a completely dark room?
probe.wrong_answer: Because my eyes haven't looked at it yet.

subject: science
statement: Light reflects off a mirror only when it hits at a specific angle.
why: Students often generalize from experiences with balls bouncing off walls where only certain angles seem to 'work'.
fix: Light reflects off a mirror at every angle; the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.

probe.question: If you shine a laser at a mirror at a 30-degree angle, what happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The light just stops or gets absorbed because it's not the right angle.

subject: science
statement: Rough surfaces do not reflect light at all.
why: Students confuse the lack of a clear image with the absence of reflection.
fix: Rough surfaces reflect light in many directions, which is called diffused reflection, allowing us to see objects from all sides.

probe.question: Why can't you see your face in a wooden table?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the table doesn't reflect any light.

subject: science
concept: Structure and Function of the Eye
statement: The pupil is a black solid spot on the surface of the eye.
why: The pupil looks like a black dot, and students lack the anatomical knowledge that it is an opening.
fix: The pupil is actually a hole in the center of the iris that allows light to enter the eye.

probe.question: What is the black circle in the middle of your eye made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a piece of black skin or a solid dot.

subject: science
statement: Stars are small objects that are stuck to the surface of the night sky.
why: Students perceive the sky as a dome or ceiling based on their visual perspective from Earth.
fix: Stars are massive, distant, self-luminous bodies located at varying distances from Earth in space.

probe.question: If you could travel to the moon, would the stars look closer?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because stars are fixed on the sky dome.

subject: science
statement: The Pole Star is the brightest star in the sky.
why: Textbooks emphasize its unique position, leading students to conflate 'special location' with 'highest magnitude'.
fix: The Pole Star is significant because it stays fixed in the north, but many other stars are much brighter.

probe.question: Is the Pole Star the most brilliant light you see at night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is the brightest star because it is the most important one.

subject: science
statement: The Moon changes shape because a shadow of the Earth falls on it.
why: Students confuse lunar phases with lunar eclipses, which are often taught together.
fix: The phases occur because we see different portions of the Moon's sunlit side as it orbits Earth.

probe.question: Why does the Moon look like a crescent sometimes?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the Earth is blocking part of the sunlight from reaching the Moon.

subject: science
statement: The Moon produces its own light like a star.
why: The Moon appears bright in the night sky, and children associate brightness with self-illumination.
fix: The Moon is a non-luminous body that reflects light coming from the Sun.

probe.question: Does the Moon have its own light source?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it glows because it is a celestial body in the sky.

subject: science
statement: Planets twinkle just like stars.
why: Students generalize the appearance of all night-sky objects as 'stars' that twinkle.
fix: Planets do not twinkle because they are much closer to Earth and appear as disks rather than point sources.

probe.question: How can you tell a planet from a star in the night sky?
probe.wrong_answer: You can't, they both twinkle.

subject: science
statement: The Sun is a planet that stays in the center of the solar system.
why: Students often categorize all celestial bodies as 'planets' due to lack of differentiation.
fix: The Sun is a star, which is a massive ball of hot gases, not a planet.

probe.question: Is the Sun a planet?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is the biggest planet in the middle of the solar system.

subject: science
statement: Distance and displacement are always the same thing.
why: In daily life, we use the terms interchangeably when describing travel between two points.
fix: Distance is the total path length covered, while displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the starting point to the finish.

probe.question: If a runner completes one full lap around a 400m circular track, what is their displacement?
probe.wrong_answer: 400 meters

subject: science
statement: An object moving at a constant speed must have a constant velocity.
why: Students often ignore the directional component of velocity, focusing only on the magnitude.
fix: Velocity includes both speed and direction; if the direction changes, the velocity changes even if the speed remains constant.

probe.question: A car turns a corner at a steady 20 km/h. Does its velocity change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the speed is constant.

subject: science
statement: If an object is moving, it must have acceleration.
why: Students confuse the state of 'being in motion' with the state of 'changing motion'.
fix: Acceleration only occurs when there is a change in velocity over time; an object moving at a steady speed in a straight line has zero acceleration.

probe.question: A train is moving at a constant 80 km/h in a straight line. What is its acceleration?
probe.wrong_answer: It is high because the train is moving fast.

subject: science
statement: The slope of a distance-time graph represents the acceleration of the object.
why: Students often conflate the visual steepness of a graph with the concept of 'getting faster'.
fix: The slope of a distance-time graph represents speed; the slope of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration.

probe.question: On a distance-time graph, what does a straight line sloping upwards indicate?
probe.wrong_answer: The object is accelerating.

subject: science
statement: An object in motion must have a force acting on it to keep moving.
why: Everyday experience shows that objects like toys or bicycles stop moving if we stop pushing them.
fix: An object will continue to move at a constant speed in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it to change its state.

probe.question: A hockey puck slides across a frictionless ice rink. What force is needed to keep it moving at a constant speed?
probe.wrong_answer: A constant forward force is needed to overcome the motion.

subject: science
statement: If an object is not moving, there are no forces acting on it.
why: Students often confuse 'no motion' with 'no forces' because they equate force only with visible movement.
fix: An object at rest can have multiple forces acting on it, but they are balanced, resulting in a net force of zero.

probe.question: A book is lying still on a table. Are there any forces acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the book is not moving.

subject: science
statement: Heavier objects have more inertia because they are harder to lift.
why: Students conflate the everyday meaning of 'heavy' (weight) with the scientific definition of inertia (resistance to change in motion).
fix: Inertia is the inherent property of an object to resist changes in its state of motion, which is directly proportional to its mass, not its weight.

probe.question: Which has more inertia: a 1kg ball on Earth or a 1kg ball in deep space?
probe.wrong_answer: The one on Earth because it is heavier.

subject: science
statement: Force is the same thing as acceleration.
why: Students often see that pushing harder (more force) makes something go faster (more acceleration) and fail to distinguish the cause from the effect.
fix: Force is the cause of the change in motion, while acceleration is the resulting rate of change of velocity.

probe.question: If an object is moving at a constant velocity, how much force is acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: It must have a constant force acting on it to keep the acceleration going.

subject: science
statement: Action-reaction forces cancel each other out so nothing can ever move.
why: Students misapply the concept of balanced forces (which act on the same object) to action-reaction pairs (which act on different objects).
fix: Action and reaction forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other out; they cause different objects to accelerate.

probe.question: A horse pulls a cart. If the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force, why does the cart move forward?
probe.wrong_answer: The cart shouldn't move because the forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel out.

subject: science
statement: Mass and weight are the same thing.
why: In everyday language, people use the terms interchangeably when buying groceries or checking body weight.
fix: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and remains constant, while weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass and changes based on location.

probe.question: If an astronaut goes to the Moon, does their mass change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they weigh less on the Moon, their mass must have decreased.

subject: science
statement: Only large objects like the Earth exert a gravitational force.
why: Students only observe the effects of gravity when objects fall toward the Earth, never between everyday small objects.
fix: Every object in the universe with mass exerts a gravitational pull on every other object, though it is only noticeable when at least one object is very massive.

probe.question: Do two pencils lying on a table exert a gravitational force on each other?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are too small and not planets.

subject: science
statement: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects.
why: Observation of falling objects like a feather and a stone in air leads to the belief that weight determines speed of fall.
fix: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of their mass.

probe.question: If you drop a heavy iron ball and a light plastic ball from the same height in a vacuum, which hits the ground first?
probe.wrong_answer: The iron ball, because it is heavier and gravity pulls it harder.

subject: science
statement: Objects float in water only if they are light.
why: Students confuse the density of an object with its total weight or mass.
fix: An object floats if its density is less than the density of the fluid it is placed in, regardless of its total mass.

probe.question: Why does a massive steel ship float while a small steel nail sinks?
probe.wrong_answer: The ship is light enough to float, but the nail is too heavy for its size.

subject: science
statement: If a person is tired after pushing a wall, they have done a lot of work.
why: Students confuse the biological effort and fatigue with the scientific definition of work.
fix: In physics, work is only done when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force.

probe.question: A student pushes a heavy cupboard for 10 minutes but it does not move. How much work is done?
probe.wrong_answer: A large amount of work because the student is sweating and tired.

subject: science
statement: Work is done whenever a force is applied to an object.
why: Students often ignore the requirement of displacement in the formula W = Fs cos(theta).
fix: Work is only done if the object actually changes its position due to the applied force.

probe.question: A man holds a heavy suitcase stationary in his hand. Is he doing work?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he is applying an upward force to hold the suitcase.

subject: science
statement: Objects at rest have no energy.
why: Students equate energy only with motion, ignoring stored potential energy.
fix: Energy can be stored in an object due to its position or configuration, which is called potential energy.

probe.question: Does a stone kept on the roof of a building have energy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not moving.

subject: science
statement: Energy is used up or lost when an object stops moving.
why: Students observe objects slowing down and assume the energy simply disappears.
fix: Energy is never lost; it is transformed into other forms like heat or sound due to friction.

probe.question: A ball rolling on the ground eventually stops. Where did its kinetic energy go?
probe.wrong_answer: It is used up and gone forever.

subject: science
statement: Power and energy are the same thing.
why: In daily life, the terms are used interchangeably to describe how 'strong' or 'active' something is.
fix: Energy is the capacity to do work, while power is the rate at which that work is done.

probe.question: If two motors do the same amount of work, do they have the same power?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they did the same amount of work.

subject: science
statement: Sound can travel through a vacuum.
why: Students often conflate light and sound because both are perceived as waves.
fix: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a material medium like air, water, or solids to propagate.

probe.question: If a bell rings inside a glass jar from which all air has been removed, will you hear it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because sound waves can travel through empty space.

subject: science
statement: Sound is a physical object that moves from the source to the ear.
why: Everyday language like 'the sound hit me' suggests sound is a projectile or a substance.
fix: Sound is a disturbance or energy transfer that causes particles of the medium to vibrate in place.

probe.question: Does the air you breathe at the source of a sound actually travel to your ear?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the air molecules move all the way from the speaker to my ear.

subject: science
statement: Sound waves move up and down like water waves.
why: Textbooks often use transverse wave diagrams to represent all waves, leading to visual confusion.
fix: Sound waves are longitudinal, meaning particles oscillate back and forth in the same direction the wave travels.

probe.question: In which direction do air particles move when a sound wave passes through them?
probe.wrong_answer: They move up and down perpendicular to the direction of the sound.

subject: science
statement: Loud sounds have a higher frequency than quiet sounds.
why: Students confuse the intensity (loudness) with the pitch (frequency) of a sound.
fix: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the wave, while pitch depends on the frequency.

probe.question: If you shout louder, what happens to the pitch of your voice?
probe.wrong_answer: The pitch gets higher because the sound is louder.

subject: science
statement: Sound travels at the same speed regardless of the material.
why: Students often assume sound is a constant property of the 'sound' itself rather than the medium.
fix: The speed of sound depends on the properties of the medium, such as density and elasticity, and is fastest in solids.

probe.question: Does sound travel faster through steel or through air?
probe.wrong_answer: It travels at the same speed in both because sound is constant.

subject: science
statement: Light reflects only off shiny, metallic surfaces like mirrors.
why: Students associate reflection exclusively with mirrors because they are the most common examples used in daily life.
fix: Reflection occurs at every boundary where light hits an object, including rough surfaces, which causes diffuse reflection.

probe.question: Can you see a wooden table in a dark room if you shine a torch on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because wood does not reflect light.

subject: science
statement: The image in a mirror is located on the surface of the glass.
why: Students confuse the physical location of the mirror with the perceived location of the virtual image behind it.
fix: The image is formed behind the mirror at a distance equal to the object's distance from the mirror.

probe.question: If you move closer to a plane mirror, where does the image move?
probe.wrong_answer: The image stays on the surface of the mirror.

subject: science
statement: A concave mirror always produces a magnified image.
why: Students often only see the 'magnifying mirror' application (like makeup mirrors) and ignore other cases.
fix: Concave mirrors produce magnified, diminished, or same-sized images depending on the object's position relative to the focus.

probe.question: What happens to the image size if an object is placed very far from a concave mirror?
probe.wrong_answer: It will still be magnified.

subject: science
statement: Light bends because it hits an object and bounces off.
why: Students conflate the mechanism of reflection with the mechanism of refraction.
fix: Refraction is the change in the speed of light as it travels from one medium to another, causing it to change direction.

probe.question: Why does a pencil look bent in a glass of water?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the light bounces off the water surface and reflects the pencil at an angle.

subject: science
statement: A higher refractive index means the material is physically harder or denser.
why: Students confuse optical density with mass density or physical hardness.
fix: Refractive index is a measure of how much light slows down in a medium, which is not always related to mass density.

probe.question: If material A has a higher refractive index than material B, is it always heavier?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it must be denser and heavier.

subject: science
statement: A lens works by blocking half of the light to create an image.
why: Students often think the 'missing' part of an image is due to the lens acting as a physical barrier.
fix: A lens refracts light from all parts of the object to converge or diverge at a specific point to form an image.

probe.question: If you cover half of a convex lens with black paper, what happens to the image?
probe.wrong_answer: Half of the image disappears.

subject: science
topic: The human eye and the colourful world
statement: A glass prism adds color to white light.
why: Students confuse the prism as a source of color rather than a tool for separation.
fix: White light is a mixture of seven colors, and the prism only separates them because each color travels at a different speed.

probe.question: If we pass white light through a prism, where do the colors come from?
probe.wrong_answer: The prism creates the colors from the white light.

subject: science
topic: The human eye and the colourful world
statement: The eye lens changes its distance from the retina to focus on objects.
why: Students often apply the camera model of focusing to the human eye.
fix: The eye lens changes its focal length by changing its curvature using ciliary muscles, not by moving back and forth.

probe.question: How does the eye focus on a near object compared to a distant one?
probe.wrong_answer: The lens moves forward or backward to adjust the distance to the retina.

subject: science
topic: The human eye and the colourful world
statement: Myopia means a person cannot see anything at all.
why: Students interpret the medical term as total blindness rather than a specific range limitation.
fix: Myopia is a condition where a person can see nearby objects clearly but distant objects appear blurry.

probe.question: What does a person with myopia experience?
probe.wrong_answer: They are completely unable to see anything.

subject: science
topic: The human eye and the colourful world
statement: The sky is blue because it reflects the blue color of the ocean.
why: This is a common cultural myth that persists despite scientific explanations.
fix: The sky appears blue because air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of sunlight (blue light) more strongly than longer wavelengths.

probe.question: Why does the sky look blue during the day?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the atmosphere reflects the blue color from the oceans.

subject: science
statement: Current is consumed by the bulb as it flows through the circuit.
why: Students often confuse the flow of electricity with the consumption of fuel like petrol or food.
fix: Current is a flow of charge that is conserved; the same amount of current enters and leaves a device.

probe.question: In a series circuit with two bulbs, is the current at point A (before the bulbs) greater than at point B (after the bulbs)?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the bulbs use up some of the current.

subject: science
statement: Batteries are sources of constant current regardless of the circuit.
why: Students generalize from the idea that a battery 'contains' electricity and pushes it out.
fix: A battery provides a constant potential difference; the current depends on the resistance of the circuit.

probe.question: If you connect a wire directly across a battery, does the current remain the same as when a bulb is connected?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the battery always pushes the same amount of current.

subject: science
statement: Voltage is a property of a single point in a circuit.
why: Textbooks often label points as '12V' or '5V' without emphasizing that this is relative to ground.
fix: Potential difference is the work done to move charge between two distinct points.

probe.question: Can a point in a circuit have a voltage without being connected to anything else?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every point has its own fixed voltage.

subject: science
statement: Resistance is a property of the current, not the conductor.
why: Students misinterpret Ohm's Law (V=IR) as R=V/I, thinking resistance changes when current changes.
fix: Resistance is an inherent property of the material and its dimensions, independent of the current flowing through it.

probe.question: If you double the voltage across a resistor, what happens to its resistance?
probe.wrong_answer: The resistance doubles because the current increases.

subject: science
statement: Adding more resistors in parallel increases the total resistance of the circuit.
why: Students intuitively apply the additive logic of series circuits to parallel ones.
fix: Adding resistors in parallel provides more paths for current, which decreases the total resistance.

probe.question: If you add a second resistor in parallel to an existing one, what happens to the total resistance?
probe.wrong_answer: It increases because there is more resistance in the circuit.

subject: science
statement: A device with a higher power rating always draws more current regardless of the voltage.
why: Students often ignore the relationship between power, voltage, and current, focusing only on the 'power' label.
fix: Power depends on both voltage and current (P=VI); a device's power rating is specific to its rated voltage.

probe.question: If two bulbs have different power ratings, does the one with higher power always have more current flowing through it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, higher power always means more current.

subject: science
statement: Magnetic field lines are physical paths or tracks that objects move along.
why: Students confuse the visual representation of field lines in diagrams with actual physical wires or paths.
fix: Magnetic field lines are imaginary lines used to represent the strength and direction of the magnetic field in a region.

probe.question: If you place a small iron filing in a magnetic field, will it always move along a curved field line?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will travel along the line like a train on a track.

subject: science
statement: Magnetic field lines start at the North pole and end at the South pole.
why: This is a common overgeneralization from the visual appearance of field lines outside the magnet.
fix: Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops that pass through the magnet from south to north, forming a complete circuit.

probe.question: Where do magnetic field lines go once they reach the South pole of a bar magnet?
probe.wrong_answer: They stop at the South pole because that is where they end.

subject: science
statement: A wire carrying current creates a magnetic field only if it is coiled.
why: Students often associate magnetism only with coils or solenoids because they are more visually distinct in experiments.
fix: Any conductor carrying an electric current produces a magnetic field around it, even if it is a straight wire.

probe.question: Does a straight copper wire carrying a steady current produce a magnetic field?
probe.wrong_answer: No, you need to coil the wire to make it magnetic.

subject: science
statement: A magnetic field exerts a force on a stationary charge.
why: Students confuse the effect of electric fields (which act on stationary charges) with magnetic fields.
fix: A magnetic field exerts a force only on a moving electric charge or a current-carrying conductor.

probe.question: Will a stationary electron placed in a strong magnetic field experience a force?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the magnetic field will push the electron.

subject: science
statement: The earth wire carries current during normal operation of an appliance.
why: Students assume that because the earth wire is connected to the appliance, it must be part of the active circuit.
fix: The earth wire is a safety feature that carries no current under normal conditions; it only conducts current to the ground if there is a fault.

probe.question: What is the primary function of the earth wire in a toaster?
probe.wrong_answer: It completes the circuit so the toaster can heat up.

subject: science
statement: A short circuit happens because the current becomes too low.
why: Students confuse the term 'short' with 'small' or 'low' based on everyday language usage.
fix: A short circuit occurs when the live and neutral wires come into direct contact, causing a sudden, very large increase in current.

probe.question: What happens to the current during a short circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: The current drops to almost zero because the path is too short.

subject: science
statement: Energy is a physical substance that gets used up when we do work.
why: Everyday language like 'running out of energy' or 'using up fuel' suggests energy is a consumable material.
fix: Energy is a property of a system that can be transferred or transformed, but it is never consumed or destroyed according to the law of conservation of energy.

probe.question: When a car runs out of petrol, where does the energy go?
probe.wrong_answer: The energy is all used up and disappears.

subject: science
concept: Formation and Nature of Fossil Fuels
statement: Fossil fuels are made from the remains of dinosaurs.
why: Popular media and cartoons often associate fossils exclusively with dinosaurs.
fix: Fossil fuels are primarily formed from the remains of ancient marine plants and microorganisms buried under layers of sediment over millions of years.

probe.question: What is the primary organic matter that turned into coal and petroleum?
probe.wrong_answer: The bones and bodies of dinosaurs.

subject: science
statement: Renewable energy sources are infinite and will never run out regardless of how much we use.
why: The term 'renewable' is often interpreted as 'limitless' in common parlance.
fix: Renewable sources are replenished by natural processes on a human timescale, but their availability at a specific location or time can still be limited.

probe.question: Can we build unlimited solar panels everywhere without any environmental impact?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because solar energy is renewable and infinite.

subject: science
statement: All renewable energy sources are completely clean and have zero environmental impact.
why: Marketing campaigns often highlight the 'green' nature of renewables while ignoring the manufacturing and disposal costs.
fix: While they produce less pollution during operation, the manufacturing, transport, and decommissioning of solar panels or wind turbines still have environmental footprints.

probe.question: Do wind farms have any negative impact on the environment?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are perfectly clean and have no impact.

subject: science
statement: A mixture always looks like a combination of different visible parts.
why: Students associate 'mixture' with kitchen examples like cereal or mixed nuts where components are distinct.
fix: A mixture can look uniform, like salt dissolved in water, where the components are mixed at a level invisible to the eye.

probe.question: Is a glass of clear salt water a mixture?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it looks like a single pure substance.

subject: science
statement: Sieving separates substances based on their weight.
why: Students confuse the action of sieving with winnowing, as both involve moving materials.
fix: Sieving separates components based on the difference in the size of their particles, not their weight.

probe.question: Why does sand pass through a sieve but pebbles stay behind?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the pebbles are heavier than the sand.

subject: science
statement: Winnowing works because the wind pushes the heavier grains away.
why: Students observe the movement of the lighter husk and incorrectly attribute the force to the heavier grain.
fix: The wind blows away the lighter husk, while the heavier grains fall straight down due to gravity.

probe.question: In winnowing, why do the grains stay near the farmer?
probe.wrong_answer: The wind is not strong enough to push the heavy grains.

subject: science
statement: Filtration removes all dissolved substances from water.
why: Students equate 'clear' water with 'pure' water, assuming the filter catches everything.
fix: Filtration only removes insoluble solid particles; dissolved substances like salt pass through the filter paper.

probe.question: If you filter salty water, will the salt remain in the filter paper?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the filter paper catches all the impurities including salt.

subject: science
statement: When water evaporates, the salt also disappears into the air.
why: Students do not see the salt left behind and assume it vanished along with the water.
fix: Evaporation turns water into vapor, but the solid salt remains behind in the container.

probe.question: What happens to the salt when you boil away all the water from a salt solution?
probe.wrong_answer: The salt evaporates with the water.

subject: science
statement: A saturated solution can hold more solute if you stir it longer.
why: Students believe that the physical act of stirring creates more space for the solute.
fix: A saturated solution has reached its limit at a specific temperature; stirring will not dissolve any more solute.

probe.question: If sugar stops dissolving in a glass of water, what should you do to dissolve more?
probe.wrong_answer: Stir it for a very long time.

subject: science
statement: All shiny materials are metals.
why: Students often associate the property of lustre exclusively with metals based on classroom demonstrations.
fix: Some non-metals like diamond or polished plastic can also appear shiny, and some metals lose their shine when they react with air.

probe.question: Is a polished piece of plastic a metal because it is shiny?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because all shiny things are metals.

subject: science
statement: Hard materials are always heavy and soft materials are always light.
why: Students confuse the property of hardness (resistance to compression) with mass or density.
fix: Hardness refers to how difficult it is to scratch or compress a material, which is independent of its weight or density.

probe.question: Is a large sponge harder than a small iron nail?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the sponge is bigger and heavier.

subject: science
statement: If a substance disappears in water, it has vanished or been destroyed.
why: Students rely on visible evidence; if they cannot see the particles, they assume the substance no longer exists.
fix: The substance breaks down into tiny particles that spread evenly throughout the water, forming a solution.

probe.question: Where does the sugar go after you stir it into water?
probe.wrong_answer: It disappears and turns into water.

subject: science
statement: Heavy objects always sink and light objects always float.
why: Everyday experiences with small objects often reinforce the idea that weight is the sole determinant of sinking.
fix: Floating and sinking depend on the material's density relative to water, not just its total weight.

probe.question: Will a heavy wooden log sink in water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is very heavy.

subject: science
statement: Transparent materials are only those that are perfectly clear like glass.
why: Students often fail to categorize materials based on the degree of light transmission, focusing only on 'perfect' examples.
fix: Materials can be transparent (clear), translucent (partially clear), or opaque (blocking light), depending on how much light passes through.

probe.question: Is butter paper transparent?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because I cannot see through it clearly.

subject: science
statement: All changes that look different are irreversible.
why: Students often confuse the visual appearance of an object with the permanence of the change.
fix: A change is reversible if the original substance can be recovered through simple physical methods, regardless of how different it looks.

probe.question: If you fold a piece of paper into a boat, can you get the paper back?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the paper has changed its shape and is now a boat.

subject: science
statement: If a change happens quickly, it must be reversible.
why: Students associate speed with the ease of undoing an action in daily life.
fix: The speed of a change has no relation to whether it can be reversed; some fast changes like burning are permanent.

probe.question: Is lighting a matchstick a reversible change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it happens very quickly.

subject: science
statement: A physical change always involves a change in the state of matter.
why: Textbooks often use melting ice as the primary example of a physical change.
fix: Physical changes include any change in shape, size, or state where no new substance is formed.

probe.question: Is cutting a piece of wood into small sawdust a physical change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the wood did not melt or freeze.

subject: science
statement: If a new color appears, it is always a chemical change.
why: Students are taught that color change is a sign of a chemical reaction, leading them to ignore physical mixing.
fix: Color change is only a sign of a chemical change if it indicates the formation of a new substance, not just mixing two colored liquids.

probe.question: If I mix blue ink and yellow ink to get green ink, is it a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the color changed.

subject: science
statement: Burning is a physical change because the object just gets smaller.
why: Students focus on the reduction in size rather than the production of ash and smoke.
fix: Burning is a chemical change because it produces entirely new substances like ash and gases that cannot be turned back into the original material.

probe.question: Why is burning a piece of paper a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not; it is just a physical change because the paper got smaller.

subject: science
statement: Rust is just dirt that collects on iron.
why: Rust looks like brown dust or soil, and students observe it accumulating on surfaces.
fix: Rust is a new substance formed by the chemical reaction between iron, oxygen, and water.

probe.question: Can you wash rust off iron like you wash off mud?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, rust is just dirty particles stuck to the metal.

subject: science
statement: Crystallisation is a chemical change because the crystals look different from the powder.
why: The dramatic change in appearance from a powder to a crystal suggests a chemical transformation to students.
fix: Crystallisation is a physical change because the substance remains the same chemically; only its physical form changes.

probe.question: Is obtaining salt crystals from a salt solution a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the salt looks like a crystal now instead of a powder.

subject: science
statement: All acids are dangerous and corrosive substances that burn everything they touch.
why: Students associate the word 'acid' with strong laboratory chemicals shown in movies or warnings.
fix: Many acids are weak and found in common food items like lemons and curd, which are safe to consume.

probe.question: Is it safe to eat a lemon?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because lemons contain acid and acids are harmful.

subject: science
statement: Litmus paper is a universal indicator that tells you exactly how acidic or basic a substance is.
why: Students often confuse the simple color change of litmus with the precise measurement provided by a pH scale.
fix: Litmus only indicates whether a substance is acidic or basic by changing color, but it does not measure the strength or pH level.

probe.question: Can you use litmus paper to tell if a solution is a strong acid or a weak acid?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, by looking at how dark the red color is on the litmus paper.

subject: science
statement: In a neutralisation reaction, the acid and base disappear completely.
why: The term 'neutralise' is interpreted as 'destroy' or 'cancel out' in everyday language.
fix: The acid and base react to form new substances, specifically a salt and water, which still exist in the container.

probe.question: After mixing equal amounts of hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, what is left in the beaker?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because they have neutralised each other and disappeared.

subject: science
statement: A pH of 0 means the substance has no acidity.
why: Students often confuse the number 0 with 'nothing' or 'zero amount' rather than a point on a logarithmic scale.
fix: A pH of 0 indicates a very strong acid; the lower the pH value below 7, the stronger the acid.

probe.question: Which is more acidic: a solution with pH 1 or a solution with pH 5?
probe.wrong_answer: pH 5 is more acidic because 5 is a larger number than 1.

subject: science
concept: Air occupies space and has mass
statement: Air is weightless and does not take up space.
why: Air is invisible and cannot be felt or seen in everyday empty containers.
fix: Air has mass and fills all available space; we can prove this by weighing a deflated versus an inflated balloon.

probe.question: If you have an empty glass bottle, what is inside it?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, it is completely empty.

subject: science
statement: Air is made up of only oxygen because that is what we breathe.
why: Students often associate air exclusively with the gas necessary for human survival.
fix: Air is a mixture of many gases, primarily nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of carbon dioxide and water vapour.

probe.question: What gases make up the air around us?
probe.wrong_answer: Only oxygen.

subject: science
statement: Smoke is a gas that is part of the air.
why: Smoke is visible in the air and is often discussed alongside air pollution.
fix: Smoke consists of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air, not a gas itself.

probe.question: Is smoke a gas like oxygen or nitrogen?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a type of gas found in polluted air.

subject: science
concept: Role of air in life processes
statement: Plants only take in carbon dioxide and never use oxygen.
why: Textbooks emphasize photosynthesis (CO2 intake) much more than plant respiration.
fix: Plants use oxygen for respiration just like animals, but they take in more carbon dioxide for photosynthesis during the day.

probe.question: Do plants need oxygen to survive?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they only need carbon dioxide.

subject: science
concept: Role of air in life processes
statement: Aquatic animals do not need air because they live in water.
why: Students confuse 'air' with 'atmospheric gas' and do not realize gases can dissolve in liquids.
fix: Aquatic animals breathe the oxygen that is dissolved in the water.

probe.question: How do fish breathe underwater?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't need air; they drink the water to get energy.

subject: science
statement: All synthetic fibres are made from plastic.
why: Students often conflate the term 'synthetic' with 'plastic' because both are human-made materials.
fix: Synthetic fibres are polymers made from chemical processes using petroleum-based raw materials, but they are distinct from the category of solid plastics used for containers.

probe.question: Is rayon a plastic?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a synthetic fibre.

subject: science
statement: Natural fibres are always better and stronger than synthetic fibres.
why: Everyday cultural emphasis on 'natural' being synonymous with 'good' or 'durable'.
fix: Synthetic fibres like nylon are often much stronger, more elastic, and more durable than natural fibres like cotton.

probe.question: Which is stronger for making a climbing rope, cotton or nylon?
probe.wrong_answer: Cotton, because it is a natural fibre.

subject: science
statement: A polymer is just a solid block of material.
why: Students struggle to visualize molecular structures and assume materials are continuous substances.
fix: A polymer is a long chain made of many repeating small units called monomers joined together.

probe.question: What is a polymer made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is made of one large, solid piece of plastic.

subject: science
statement: All plastics melt when heated.
why: General observation that most household plastic items deform under high heat.
fix: Thermoplastics can be reshaped by heating, but thermosetting plastics cannot be softened or reshaped once they are set.

probe.question: Can you melt a plastic switch cover to reshape it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all plastics melt if you make them hot enough.

subject: science
statement: Plastic is bad for the environment because it is toxic to touch.
why: Confusion between the environmental impact (persistence) and the chemical safety of the material.
fix: Plastics are harmful to the environment primarily because they are non-biodegradable and persist for centuries, not because they are inherently poisonous to touch.

probe.question: Why should we avoid using plastic bags?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are poisonous and will make us sick if we touch them.

subject: science
concept: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
statement: All metals are always solid at room temperature.
why: Students generalize from common metals like iron and copper seen in daily life.
fix: Mercury is a metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature.

probe.question: Is mercury a metal?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is a liquid.

subject: science
concept: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
statement: Non-metals are always gases.
why: Students often associate non-metals with oxygen or nitrogen in the air.
fix: Non-metals can be solids (like carbon or sulfur) or liquids (like bromine) in addition to gases.

probe.question: Is sulfur a non-metal?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is a solid.

subject: science
concept: Chemical Reactions with Oxygen and Water
statement: Metal oxides are always acidic in nature.
why: Students confuse metal oxides with non-metal oxides which form acids in water.
fix: Metal oxides are generally basic, while non-metal oxides are generally acidic.

probe.question: What happens when magnesium oxide is dissolved in water and tested with litmus?
probe.wrong_answer: It turns blue litmus red because it is an oxide.

subject: science
statement: Any metal can displace another metal from its salt solution.
why: Students assume that if a reaction happens between two metals, it will always happen regardless of which is the salt.
fix: Only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

probe.question: Will copper displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because both are metals and they react.

subject: science
statement: Natural resources like coal and petroleum will never run out because the Earth is huge.
why: Students often equate the vastness of the planet with an infinite supply of materials.
fix: These resources are finite because they take millions of years to form and are being consumed much faster than they can be replenished.

probe.question: If we keep using petrol for cars every day, will it ever finish?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the Earth has a huge underground supply that will last forever.

subject: science
statement: Fossil fuels are formed from the remains of dinosaurs.
why: Popular media and cartoons often associate fossils exclusively with dinosaurs.
fix: Coal is formed primarily from the remains of ancient land plants, while petroleum is formed from tiny marine organisms.

probe.question: What kind of living things turned into coal millions of years ago?
probe.wrong_answer: Dinosaurs that died and got buried under the ground.

subject: science
statement: Fossil fuels are created by the Earth heating up rocks.
why: Students confuse the geological heat and pressure with the process of cooking or burning.
fix: Fossil fuels are formed by the slow chemical transformation of organic matter under immense pressure and heat over millions of years.

probe.question: How does coal form underground?
probe.wrong_answer: The Earth's heat melts rocks and turns them into coal.

subject: science
statement: Petroleum is a single substance that is used directly in cars.
why: Students see 'petrol' and 'petroleum' used interchangeably in daily life.
fix: Petroleum is a dark, oily liquid mixture that must be refined into separate components like petrol, diesel, and kerosene.

probe.question: What is crude oil?
probe.wrong_answer: It is just another name for the petrol we put in our bikes.

subject: science
statement: Only solids can be combustible substances.
why: Students often associate combustion with burning wood or paper, ignoring fuels they cannot easily see or touch.
fix: Combustion is a chemical reaction with oxygen that can occur with solids, liquids, and gases like LPG or hydrogen.

probe.question: Is cooking gas (LPG) a combustible substance?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is a gas, not a solid material.

subject: science
statement: Combustion is the same thing as melting.
why: Students often confuse the physical change of a candle wax melting with the chemical process of the wick burning.
fix: Combustion is a chemical reaction that produces new substances like carbon dioxide and water, whereas melting is just a change of state.

probe.question: What happens to a candle when it burns?
probe.wrong_answer: The wax melts and disappears into the air.

subject: science
statement: A substance will catch fire as soon as it is near a flame.
why: Students observe that fires start quickly and ignore the threshold temperature required for the reaction to begin.
fix: A substance only starts burning when it reaches its specific ignition temperature, which varies for different materials.

probe.question: Why does a paper cup with water not burn when placed over a flame?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the paper is not a good fuel.

subject: science
statement: The blue part of a flame is the coolest part.
why: Students often associate blue with 'cold' (like ice) and red/orange with 'hot' (like the sun or fire).
fix: The blue zone represents complete combustion and is actually the hottest part of the flame.

probe.question: If you want to heat a metal wire quickly, which part of the flame should you use?
probe.wrong_answer: The yellow part, because it looks brighter and hotter.

subject: science
statement: All fuels produce the same amount of heat when burned.
why: Students tend to focus on the act of burning rather than the energy content per unit mass of the fuel.
fix: Different fuels have different calorific values, meaning they release different amounts of heat energy for the same quantity.

probe.question: If you burn 1kg of wood and 1kg of LPG, will they produce the same heat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the weight of the fuel is the same.

subject: science
statement: Matter is continuous and does not consist of discrete particles.
why: Our senses perceive objects like water or wood as smooth, unbroken wholes rather than collections of tiny particles.
fix: All matter is composed of extremely small, invisible particles that have space between them.

probe.question: If you dissolve salt in water, where does the salt go?
probe.wrong_answer: The salt disappears or melts into the water to become part of a continuous liquid.

subject: science
